Air resistance is negligible. Rank the horizontal distances traveled before landing at the launch level from greatest to least.

options.why: Ranks by the launch speed alone.
Ranks by the launch angle alone, as if a steeper launch always goes farther.
Ranks by $v^2\cos\theta$, treating the horizontal speed times the speed as the range.
The range is $v^2\sin2\theta/g$, so the ranges are A: 40.8 m, B: 11.5 m, C: 12.7 m, D: 16.5 m, which ranks as A > D > C > B.

ap_physics_1-m02.stem: A student launches a ball from level ground at a fixed angle of $45^\circ$ above the horizontal with several different speeds and measures the horizontal distance traveled before the ball lands at the launch level. The table shows the speed and the range for five trials. Which of the following is best supported by the data?

stimulus.description: Launch speed and range of a ball

options.text: The range is nearly the same in every trial, so it does not depend on the launch speed.
options.why: Overlooks that the range rises from $6.61\text{ m}$ to $26.53\text{ m}$ as the speed increases.

options.text: The ratio $R/v$ is nearly the same in every trial, so the range is proportional to the launch speed.
options.why: Tests $R/v$, but it rises from $0.826$ to $1.66\text{ s}$ as the speed increases.

options.text: The product $Rv$ is nearly constant, so a faster launch gives a shorter range.
options.why: Tests the product, but the product increases with the speed.

options.text: The ratio $R/v^2$ is nearly the same in every trial, about $0.102\text{ s}^2/\text{m}$, so the range is proportional to the square of the launch speed.
options.why: The values of $R/v^2$ range only from $0.100$ to $0.104\text{ s}^2/\text{m}$, so $R\propto v^2$ at a fixed angle.

ap_physics_1-m03.stem: A $3\text{ kg}$ firework shell is launched from level ground and would land $30\text{ m}$ from the launch point if it did not explode. At the top of its path the shell explodes into two fragments of masses $1.5\text{ kg}$ and $1.5\text{ kg}$. Both fragments land on the ground at the same time. The $1.5\text{ kg}$ fragment lands $20\text{ m}$ from the launch point. Air resistance is negligible. Which statement about the other fragment is correct and best justified?

options.text: The $1.5\text{ kg}$ fragment lands $30\text{ m}$ from the launch point, because the shell was headed there before the explosion.
options.why: Assumes that each fragment follows the original path, ignoring that the internal forces change the fragment trajectories while keeping the center of mass path.

options.text: The position of the second fragment cannot be found, because the explosion forces are unknown.
options.why: Thinks the explosion forces must be known, but they are internal forces that do not change the motion of the center of mass.

options.text: The $1.5\text{ kg}$ fragment lands $40.0\text{ m}$ from the launch point, because the explosion forces are internal, so the center of mass of the two fragments still lands $30\text{ m}$ from the launch point.
options.why: The center of mass lands at $30\text{ m}$: $(1.5)(20)+(1.5)x_2=(3)(30)$, so $x_2=40.0\text{ m}$.

options.text: The $1.5\text{ kg}$ fragment lands $40.0\text{ m}$ from the launch point, because the two fragments land symmetrically about $30\text{ m}$.
options.why: Uses a symmetric landing distance without weighting by the masses.

key_conditions.evidence: the stem says both fragments land at the same time and air resistance is negligible

The table shows the speed and the tension for five trials. Which of the following is best supported by the data?

stimulus.description: Speed and string tension for a ball in a horizontal circle

options.text: The tension is nearly the same in every trial, so it does not depend on the speed.
options.why: Overlooks that the tension rises from $1.139\text{ N}$ to $8.125\text{ N}$ as the speed increases.

options.text: The ratio $F/v$ is nearly the same in every trial, so the tension is proportional to the speed.
options.why: Tests $F/v$, but it rises from $0.759$ to $2.03\text{ N s/m}$ as the speed increases.

options.text: The product $Fv$ is nearly constant, so a faster ball needs less tension.

options.text: The ratio $F/v^2$ is nearly the same in every trial, about $0.498\text{ N s}^2/\text{m}^2$, so the tension is proportional to the square of the speed.
options.why: The values of $F/v^2$ range only from $0.491$ to $0.508\text{ N s}^2/\text{m}^2$, so $F\propto v^2$ (as in $F=mv^2/r$).

ap_physics_1-m05.stem: A block of mass $m$ is released from rest at the top of an incline that makes an angle $\theta$ with the horizontal. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the incline is $\mu$. Which of the following is the speed of the block after it has slid a distance $d$ down the incline?

options.why: The net force along the incline is $mg\sin\theta-\mu mg\cos\theta$, so $a=g(\sin\theta-\mu\cos\theta)$ and $v=\sqrt{2ad}$ (or the work-energy theorem $mgd\sin\theta-\mu mg\cos\theta\,d=\tfrac12mv^2$).
Leaves out the square root.
Ignores friction.
Adds the friction term instead of subtracting it.

ap_physics_1-m06.stem: A block of mass $m$ is released from rest at a height $h$ above the free end of a light vertical spring of spring constant $k$ that stands on the floor. The block falls onto the spring and compresses it. Which of the following is the maximum compression of the spring?

options.why: Energy is conserved from release to the lowest point: $mg(h+x)=\tfrac12kx^2$, a quadratic whose positive root is $x=\dfrac{mg+\sqrt{m^2g^2+2kmgh}}{k}$.
Takes the other root of the quadratic, which subtracts $mg$.
Forgets that the block keeps falling while it compresses the spring: $mgh=\tfrac12kx^2$.
Balances only the weight with the spring force, $kx=mg$.

ap_physics_1-m07.stem: A truck cruises at a constant speed of $20\text{ m/s}$ on a level road while its engine delivers a constant power. The total resistive force on the truck is $1000\text{ N}$. On a rougher stretch of road the total resistive force is $4$ times as great, and the engine delivers the same power. What is the best prediction of the constant speed of the truck on the rougher road?

options.why: Multiplies the speed by the factor for the resistive force.
Keeps the speed the same because the power is the same.
At constant speed the engine force equals the resistive force, so $P=Fv$. With the same power, $v_2=P/F_2=20.0/4=5.00\text{ m/s}$.
Divides the speed by the square of the factor.

ap_physics_1-m08.stem: A bullet of mass $m$ is fired horizontally into a block of mass $M$ that hangs at rest from a light string and embeds in the block. The block and bullet swing up together to a maximum height $h$ above the starting position. Which of the following is the speed of the bullet just before it hits the block?

options.why: Momentum is conserved in the collision, $mv=(m+M)V$, and energy is conserved during the swing, $V=\sqrt{2gh}$, so $v=\dfrac{m+M}{m}\sqrt{2gh}$.
Leaves out the square root.
Ignores the momentum transfer and uses only the energy of the block, $\sqrt{2gh}$.
Inverts the mass ratio.

key_conditions.evidence: the stem says the bullet embeds in the block and the block swings up on a light string

misconceptions.description: Leaves out the square root.

Inverts the mass ratio.

verification.independent_path: the height is computed forward from the bullet speed with momentum and energy conservation, and the printed option is evaluated by a TeX evaluator to recover the speed

ap_physics_1-m09.stem: A solid sphere and a hoop, with the same mass and radius, are released from rest at the same time at the top of an incline of height $1.5\text{ m}$. Both roll without slipping. Which statement about the objects at the bottom of the incline is correct and best justified?

options.text: The solid sphere is moving faster ($4.58\text{ m/s}$ compared with $3.83\text{ m/s}$) because it has the smaller rotational inertia, so a smaller share of the same energy lost by gravity goes into rotation.
options.why: With $mgh=\tfrac12mv^2(1+I/mR^2)$ the speed is $\sqrt{2gh/(1+k)}$ with $k=0.4$ for the solid sphere and $k=1$ for the hoop.

options.text: The two objects are moving at the same speed, because they have the same mass, radius and starting height.
options.why: Assumes that the same mass and height give the same speed, ignoring that the energy is shared between rotation and translation differently.

options.text: The hoop is moving faster, because its larger rotational inertia gives it more energy at the bottom.
options.why: Thinks a larger rotational inertia gives more total energy; the total energy is the same for both objects.

options.text: The solid sphere is moving faster, because it has the larger rotational inertia and so more energy is available for translation.
options.why: Reverses the effect of the rotational inertia on the share of energy in translation.

blueprint.concept: Justifying which rolling object is faster from the share of energy that goes into rotation

Compare the share of the energy that stays in translation for the two shapes

key_conditions.condition: both objects roll without slipping from the same height
key_conditions.evidence: the stem says both roll without slipping from rest at the top of the same incline

misconceptions.description: Assumes that the same mass and height give the same speed, ignoring that the energy is shared between rotation and translation differently.
Thinks a larger rotational inertia gives more total energy; the total energy is the same for both objects.
Reverses the effect of the rotational inertia on the share of energy in translation.

verification.independent_path: the speeds are computed from energy conservation with the rotational inertia factors and compared

ap_physics_1-m10.stem: A block of mass $1\text{ kg}$ oscillates on a horizontal frictionless surface at the end of a spring of spring constant $80\text{ N/m}$ with an amplitude of $20\text{ cm}$. Its maximum speed is $1.79\text{ m/s}$. The block is replaced by one with $4$ times the mass and set oscillating on the same spring with $3$ times the amplitude. What is the best prediction of the new maximum speed?

options.why: Scales the speed with the amplitude factor only.
Divides by the mass factor instead of its square root.
Energy conservation gives $\tfrac12kA^2=\tfrac12mv_{max}^2$, so $v_{max}=A\sqrt{k/m}$ and the new speed is $1.79\times3/\sqrt{4}=2.68\text{ m/s}$.
Multiplies by the amplitude factor and by the square root of the mass factor.

ap_physics_1-m11.stem: Four solid objects are each completely submerged and held at rest in a different liquid (mass, volume, liquid and its density): A: $0.8\text{ kg}$, $250\text{ cm}^3$, in alcohol ($800\text{ kg/m}^3$); B: $2\text{ kg}$, $100\text{ cm}^3$, in glycerin ($1260\text{ kg/m}^3$); C: $0.3\text{ kg}$, $150\text{ cm}^3$, in water ($1000\text{ kg/m}^3$); D: $0.5\text{ kg}$, $300\text{ cm}^3$, in brine ($1200\text{ kg/m}^3$). Rank the magnitudes of the buoyant forces on the objects from greatest to least.

options.why: Ranks by the mass of the object, as if a heavier object gets a larger buoyant force.
The buoyant force is $\rho_{fluid}Vg$, so the forces are A: 1.96 N, B: 1.23 N, C: 1.47 N, D: 3.53 N, which ranks as D > A > C > B.
Ranks by the density of the fluid alone.
Ranks by the weight of the object minus nothing, $mg/V$, the object's density.

student_thinking: Use $F_B=\rho_{fluid}Vg$ with the volume converted to cubic meters
Order the four forces

key_conditions.condition: each object is completely submerged
key_conditions.evidence: the stem says each object is completely submerged

misconceptions.description: Ranks by the mass of the object, as if a heavier object gets a larger buoyant force.
Ranks by the weight of the object minus nothing, $mg/V$, the object's density.

verification.independent_path: exact fractions of the density times the volume are sorted and compared with the floating-point ordering

ap_physics_1-m12.stem: Three open containers have different shapes: a wide cylinder, a narrow tube, and a container that widens toward the top. Each is filled with the same liquid (density $1000\text{ kg/m}^3$) to the same depth of $0.5\text{ m}$ and rests on a table. The surrounding air pressure is $101.3\text{ kPa}$. Which statement about the pressure at the bottom of the containers is correct and best justified?

options.text: The pressure at the bottom is the same in all three containers, $106\text{ kPa}$, because it depends only on the depth and density of the liquid and the air pressure above it, not on the shape or the amount of liquid.
options.why: $P=P_0+\rho gh=101.3\text{ kPa}+(1000)(9.8)(0.5)=106\text{ kPa}$ for every container.

options.text: The pressure is greatest in the container that widens toward the top, because there is more liquid above the sides.
options.why: Uses the amount of liquid above the sides rather than the depth of the liquid above the bottom.

options.text: The pressure is greatest in the wide cylinder, because it holds the most liquid and the liquid there weighs the most.
options.why: Confuses the total weight of the liquid with the pressure, which depends on the depth.

options.text: The pressure is greatest in the narrow tube, because the same force is spread over a smaller area.
options.why: Applies the idea that pressure is force over area to the base area instead of using the depth and density of the liquid.

verification.independent_path: the bottom pressure is computed from the air pressure plus the hydrostatic term with the same depth and density and is the same for all three shapes

ap_physics_1-m13.stem: A student lowers a pressure sensor to different depths in a deep tank of liquid that is open to the air and records the absolute pressure at each depth. The table shows the depth and the absolute pressure for five trials. Which of the following is best supported by the data?

stimulus.description: Depth and absolute pressure in a liquid

options.text: The pressure is nearly the same at every depth, so the pressure does not depend on the depth of the sensor.
options.why: Overlooks that the pressure rises from $113.0\text{ kPa}$ to $148.4\text{ kPa}$ as the depth increases.

options.text: The ratio $P/h$ is nearly the same in every trial, so the absolute pressure is proportional to the depth of the sensor.
options.why: Tests $P/h$, but it falls from $113$ to $37.1\text{ kPa/m}$ because the air pressure at the surface is part of every reading.

options.text: The product $Ph$ is nearly constant, so a deeper sensor reads a lower absolute pressure in the liquid.
options.why: Tests the product, but the product increases with the depth.

options.text: The pressure rises by about $11.7\text{ kPa}$ for each meter of depth in every trial, so the pressure increases linearly with depth.
options.why: The values of $(P-101.3)/h$ range only from $11.7$ to $11.8\text{ kPa/m}$, so $P=P_0+\rho gh$ with $\rho g\approx11.7\text{ kPa/m}$.

blueprint.subject: ap_physics_1
blueprint.concept: Supporting the linear increase of pressure with depth from data that include the surface pressure
student_thinking: Subtract the surface pressure and divide by the depth for each trial
Decide which ratio is nearly constant and what that says about the relationship

key_conditions.condition: the liquid is at rest and open to the air
key_conditions.evidence: the stem says the tank is open to the air and the liquid is deep

misconceptions.description: Overlooks that the pressure rises from $113.0\text{ kPa}$ to $148.4\text{ kPa}$ as the depth increases.
Tests $P/h$, but it falls from $113$ to $37.1\text{ kPa/m}$ because the air pressure at the surface is part of every reading.
Tests the product, but the product increases with the depth.

verification.independent_path: the slope of pressure against depth from the normal equations agrees with the mean of the increases divided by the depth, and P/h is not constant
